rv.q: If this is a jukebox musical, this is how you do it right.
The results are diverting, even if they don't quite match the effervescence of that last excursion.
The newly manufactured 1920s-set musical 'Nice Work if You It' crams vintage Gershwin songs into a bubbly crowdpleaser, enchantingly rendered by thesps Kelli O'Hara, Michael McGrath and Judy Kaye.
Overall, the show is too afraid of emotional engagement, which is silly when you have these songs and O'Hara's voice and Broderick's likable self to deliver them.
An alternative title for “Nice Work” might be “It Lukewarm.”
Every detail in “Nice Work If You It” is finely tuned and beautifully turned out.

Who says they don't write Broadway musicals like they used to? Joe DiPietro and Kathleen Marshall have teamed up to reshuffle the Gershwin playlist into a new musical...that is quite simply, to borrow another song title, 'Delishious.'

Matthew Broderick, who hasn’t enjoyed much success on Broadway since "The Producers" a decade ago, manages to redeem himself in "Nice Work If You It," a "new" Gershwin musical also starring Kelli O’Hara and other stage veterans who bring down the house in supporting comedic roles.
It's as joyfully airheaded and kitschy as a drag show, which should make it a must-see for anyone with a more-is-more stance on sequins.

True, Nice Work If You It (* * * out of four) doesn't use an inane story line to simply string together a beloved band or singer's catalog or a bunch of disparate rock chestnuts. Instead, it uses an inane story line to string together the timeless songs of George and Ira Gershwin. ... Broder...
If only the story hadn’t dragged on and on with multiple endings, “Nice Work” would have made for a nicer evening, away from work.
The result is mostly a flop-sweat inducing affair.
But Marshall hamstrings them all, with arid staging, flaccid pacing, and witless choreography that makes even the peppiest numbers feel leaden.

They've managed to take about 20 songs from the George Gershwin and Ira Gershwin catalog, marry them to the skeleton of the 1926 musical 'O, Kay!' and emerge with a plot that makes madcap sense with songs that feel right for the occasion.
The show is a perfectly pleasant throwback to the kind of musical theater that Broadway used to do routinely — but it's also the kind of show that makes you realize why Broadway had to evolve.

cn.t: A pleasant but lightweight Gershwin pastiche that charms in spots but feels dutiful overall. Broderick and O'Hara appeal individually though lack romantic spark, while Marshall's direction and period trappings deliver old-fashioned entertainment.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Imperial Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
A noticeable side angle, but Imperial Theatre's more moderate size keeps the distance from the stage manageable.

vs.sum: The Imperial Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and solid sound quality, though some seats may miss minor stage action. While the ambiance is enhanced by its historic architectural design, comfort is average with decent legroom. Facilities are lacking, with long restroom lines being a common issue.
